title: Indonesian Firefighters Teach Fire Safety Set to 'Saajan Ji Ghar Aaye' in Viral Videos
excerpt: Fire and rescue crews in Makassar, Indonesia have gone viral for demonstrating how to handle kitchen and gas-cylinder fires while Bollywood songs play — turning a routine safety drill into the internet's favorite music video.
body:
• Firefighters in Makassar, Indonesia have gone viral for fire-safety demonstration videos set to Bollywood songs, including the Kuch Kuch Hota Hai classic "Saajan Ji Ghar Aaye."
  • One clip shows how to smother a burning cooking vessel with a wet cloth — never water — while another demonstrates the same technique on a gas cylinder fire.
  • The videos were posted on Instagram by fire and rescue worker @tamsildanuarta and amplified on X by @sougat18, drawing praise for making safety lessons memorable.
  • They arrive as Indonesia battles severe peatland wildfires that have driven respiratory infections sharply higher, according to the country's Health Ministry.

A fire safety drill in Indonesia has found an unlikely soundtrack — a 1990s Bollywood wedding anthem. Firefighters in Makassar have gone viral for Instagram videos demonstrating basic fire safety set to Hindi film songs, including "Saajan Ji Ghar Aaye" from Kuch Kuch Hota Hai.

The clips were posted by @tamsildanuarta, a fire and rescue department worker, and shared widely on X by @sougat18. According to News18, the pairing of a serious drill with a familiar Bollywood hit has delighted viewers well beyond Indonesia.

The videos

In one clip, "Teri Aankhon Ko Aankhon Se" plays while a firefighter demonstrates what to do when a cooking vessel catches fire: do not pour water directly onto it. Instead, the firefighter drapes a wet cloth over the flames to smother them, according to Khel Ja's coverage.

The second video opens with "Tere Ghar Aaya Mai Aaya Tujhko Lene" — the opening line of "Saajan Ji Ghar Aaye" — and tackles the more dangerous case of a gas cylinder fire. The firefighter again shows that water should not be used on a burning cylinder, demonstrating how a wet cloth can contain the flames.

The song choice is instantly recognizable across Southeast Asia. "Saajan Ji Ghar Aaye" comes from Kuch Kuch Hota Hai, Karan Johar's 1998 directorial debut starring Shah Rukh Khan, Kajol and Rani Mukerji, with Salman Khan in a special appearance as Aman Mehra. Sung by Alka Yagnik, Kumar Sanu and Kavita Krishnamurthy, the wedding number became one of the defining tracks of 1990s Bollywood.

"In the Multiverse Impossible things: Indonesia-based Firefighters are teaching Fire Safety Basics on Instagram using Bollywood Songs."

— @sougat18, on X

Why the format works

Fire safety instruction has a known problem: it is dry, and dry gets ignored. The Makassar firefighters have landed on a lean formula: a genuine professional, a real flame, and a song the audience already knows by heart.

Bollywood has a deep following in Indonesia, where Hindi films have aired on local television dubbed in Bahasa Indonesia for years and stars like Shah Rukh Khan are household names. When the soundtrack is already in the viewer's head, the safety lesson rides along with it.

The reaction suggests the bet is paying off. "Hahaha, that's a fun (and I believe very effective) way to educate people about the subject," one commenter wrote, according to Khel Ja.

"Hahaha, that's a fun (and I believe very effective) way to educate people about the subject."

— A commenter reacting to the videos on X

A serious backdrop

The light-hearted videos land in a country where fire safety is anything but abstract right now. Indonesia is in the middle of a severe wildfire season: more than 50,000 respiratory infections have been linked to peatland fires, with cases doubling in a single week in early September, according to the Health Ministry and reported by Reuters. The EU's Copernicus service found Indonesia's August fire emissions were the highest recorded in that month for 24 years.

The viral kitchen demos address household accidents rather than peatland blazes, but they arrive when fire awareness is at the front of Indonesia's national conversation. A safety message people actually watch and share is a safety message that works.

The diaspora connection

For Indian diaspora audiences, the videos are a small window into Bollywood's soft power. A fire department worker in Sulawesi choosing a 1998 Hindi film song as his drill soundtrack — and millions of viewers getting the joke instantly — speaks to the durability of Bollywood's cultural reach. It is the kind of crossover diaspora communities live in every day: home culture showing up in unexpected places, untranslated and immediately understood.

What's next

The clips will almost certainly spawn imitators — fire departments and civic agencies in both Indonesia and India now have a proven template. The @tamsildanuarta account has the formula down: real technique, real calm, familiar music. If the series continues, it could become one of the more effective public-safety campaigns of the social media era — proof that the best way to make people remember how to put out a fire is to give them a song they can't forget.
image_caption: Firefighters work to contain peatland fires in South Sumatra, Indonesia, during the country's severe wildfire season. Health officials say more than 50,000 respiratory infections have been linked to the fires so far.
